items.title: Audit trail & activity logging

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

items.body:
## Situation

Nothing on the platform currently records who did what. Each product module writes its own domain rows and, at best, a `created_by`/`updated_by` column that is overwritten on the next edit. There is no record of a read at all — and in healthcare, reads are the sensitive event. A ward nurse opening a colleague's family member's discharge summary, a TPA co-ordinator browsing claims outside their assigned batch, a pharmacist viewing a psychiatric prescription unrelated to any dispense — all of these are invisible.

This blocks several things simultaneously. NABH and NABL accreditation assessors expect evidence that record access is controlled and traceable. Under the DPDP Act 2023 a data principal may ask a hospital what has been done with their personal data, and the hospital cannot answer without an access log. CERT-In directions impose log-retention obligations that a 30-day application log tier does not satisfy. Break-glass emergency access — deliberately designed to bypass the normal care-relationship check in OpenFGA — is only defensible if every use is recorded and reviewed; without that record, break-glass is simply an unaudited backdoor. And #52 SIEM has nothing to detect against, because detection needs a stream of normalised access events that does not exist.

Affected: hospital admins and DPOs who must answer for access, ward nurses and clinicians whose legitimate access must be distinguishable from misuse, pathologists and pharmacists handling regulated categories, and the platform security team.

---

## Task

### User or System Story

**As a** hospital DPO, accreditation assessor and platform security engineer
**I want** every security- and clinically-significant action across all eleven products emitted as a canonical audit event and durably stored
**So that** record access, changes, prescriptions, billing, refunds, inventory movements, permission changes, exports and break-glass use are all attributable, retained and available for review.

### Scope

**In scope**

* A canonical audit event schema and a shared Go library (`pkg/audit`) used by every module — one shape, one emitter, no per-module variants.
* Automatic emission at the tenant-scoped data-access layer for reads and writes on classified entities, so a developer cannot add a new PHI query path that skips auditing.
* Explicit emission for the enumerated high-value actions: login and session events, patient-record access, record updates, prescription create/amend/cancel, billing changes, refunds, inventory adjustments, permission and role changes, data exports, and break-glass activation.
* Field-level change capture on writes: which fields changed, old and new values for non-PHI fields, and value hashes for PHI fields.
* Durable transport on NATS JetStream (`audit.>`) with an outbox in the originating transaction so an audit event is never lost when the business write commits.
* Partitioned PostgreSQL storage with a retention policy per event class, driven by the Country Profile.
* Break-glass events carry the declared reason, the patient, the bypassed relation and the expiry of the temporary grant.
* Mobile clients emit audit events for offline actions with both the client action time and the sync time.

**Out of scope**

* Cryptographic hash chaining and integrity verification of the stored records — owned by #436 Tamper-evident audit records.
* Search UI, filters, saved queries and accreditation report generation — owned by #437 Audit search and reporting.
* The per-record change-history timeline surfaced to clinicians and patients — owned by #55 Data access & change history log, which is a read model built over this stream.
* Detection rules and alerting over the stream — owned by #52 SIEM / security monitoring.
* The DPDP data-principal access-request workflow that consumes these records — owned by the Privacy and Compliance epic.

---

## Recommended Solution

**Emit at the choke point, not at the call sites.** The platform already mandates a single tenant-scoped data-access layer so no query can omit its tenant. Extend that same layer with audit emission. A GORM callback registered on the tenant-scoped session inspects the model's registered classification and emits on `AfterQuery`, `AfterCreate`, `AfterUpdate` and `AfterDelete`. Entities opt in via an interface, and a CI check fails the build if a model tagged `phi` or `pii` in the classification registry does not implement it. Relying on developers to remember an `audit.Log(...)` call at 400 call sites is the failure mode this design exists to avoid.

**Canonical event.**

```json
{
  "audit_id": "01J8ZQ...",
  "schema_version": 1,
  "occurred_at": "2026-07-20T09:14:22.113Z",
  "recorded_at": "2026-07-20T09:14:22.140Z",
  "tenant_id": "t-apollo",
  "facility_id": "f-12",
  "actor": {"subject": "kc:8f3a", "role": "ward_nurse", "on_behalf_of": null,
            "session_id": "s-91", "client": "medicore-web", "source_ip": "203.0.113.44"},
  "action": "record.read",
  "category": "phi_access",
  "resource": {"type": "Encounter", "id": "enc_7712", "patient_id": "pat_4410"},
  "outcome": "allow",
  "authorisation": {"decision_path": "care_team", "break_glass": false, "consent_artefact": "ca_88"},
  "changes": [{"field": "discharge_summary", "old_hash": "sha256:...", "new_hash": "sha256:...", "phi": true},
              {"field": "bed_id", "old": "B-12", "new": "B-19", "phi": false}],
  "trace_id": "4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736"
}
```

`occurred_at` versus `recorded_at` is what makes offline mobile capture honest — a CareConnect home-visit nurse working without signal produces events whose occurrence precedes recording by hours, and both times must be preserved rather than reconciled away.

**Delivery guarantee.** Audit emission must not be best-effort, and it must not fail the clinical write. Use a transactional outbox: the GORM callback writes an `audit_outbox` row inside the same transaction as the business change, and a relay publishes to JetStream and marks it dispatched. For pure reads there is no business transaction, so reads publish directly with a bounded local disk buffer for JetStream unavailability. Reads are the higher-volume, lower-consequence case; writes get the stronger guarantee.

```sql
CREATE TABLE audit_event (
  audit_id     uuid NOT NULL,
  occurred_at  timestamptz NOT NULL,
  recorded_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  tenant_id    text NOT NULL,
  facility_id  text,
  actor_sub    text NOT NULL,
  actor_role   text,
  on_behalf_of text,
  action       text NOT NULL,
  category     text NOT NULL CHECK (category IN
      ('auth','phi_access','record_change','prescription','billing','refund',
       'inventory','permission','export','break_glass','facility','safety')),
  resource_type text, resource_id text, patient_id text,
  outcome      text NOT NULL CHECK (outcome IN ('allow','deny','error')),
  break_glass  boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false,
  changes      jsonb,
  trace_id     text,
  PRIMARY KEY (occurred_at, audit_id)
) PARTITION BY RANGE (occurred_at);

CREATE INDEX ON audit_event (tenant_id, patient_id, occurred_at DESC);
CREATE INDEX ON audit_event (tenant_id, actor_sub, occurred_at DESC);
CREATE INDEX ON audit_event (tenant_id, category, occurred_at DESC) WHERE break_glass;
```

RLS is enabled on `audit_event` with the same tenant policy as clinical tables — but the table grants no `UPDATE` or `DELETE` to the application role at all. Audit records are append-only at the privilege level, which is a cheap and independent control that holds even before #436's hash chain lands. Retention deletion happens by dropping whole partitions under a separate maintenance role.

**API surface** (write path is internal; these are the read/administrative endpoints this story owns):

* `POST /internal/v1/audit/events` — batch ingest for clients that cannot use the data layer (mobile sync, external integrations); authenticated by service identity.
* `GET  /api/v1/audit/events?patient_id=&actor=&category=&from=&to=` — raw event access for platform security and tenant DPO.
* `GET  /api/v1/audit/events/{id}`
* `GET  /api/v1/audit/coverage` — operational endpoint reporting which registered entities are emitting, used by the CI coverage gate.

**Events published.** `audit.<category>.<action>` on JetStream, e.g. `audit.phi_access.record.read`, `audit.break_glass.activated`, `audit.permission.role_granted`, `audit.export.completed`. Consumed by #52 (detection), #55 (change-history read model), #436 (hash chain), #437 (search index). Retention on the stream is short — the durable copy is PostgreSQL; JetStream is transport, not storage.

**Authorisation.**

```
type audit_event
  relations
    define tenant: [tenant]
    define subject_patient: [patient]
    define platform_security: [team#member]
    define tenant_dpo: dpo from tenant
    define can_view: platform_security or tenant_dpo
```

Deliberately, a clinician cannot query the raw audit stream — that is a surveillance capability. Clinicians see only the per-record history from #55, scoped to records they are already authorised to view.

**Sequencing.** Must land early; #52, #55, #436 and #437 all depend on it. Requires the data classification registry and the tenant-scoped data-access layer to exist first. The OpenFGA decision-path field requires the authorisation service to expose why a check passed, which may need a small change there.

**Risks.** Audit volume on the read path is the main cost and latency risk — a busy 500-bed hospital generates millions of read events daily. Mitigated by emitting one event per logical resource access rather than per row (a chart open is one `Encounter` read, not forty `Observation` reads), by asynchronous publication off the request path, and by a p95 added-latency budget of 3 ms enforced in a benchmark test. The second risk is PHI leaking into audit payloads, which would make the audit store a second, less-protected copy of the record; mitigated by hashing rather than storing values for any field classified PHI, and by a unit test over the classification registry asserting no `phi` field can serialise a raw value into `changes`.

---

## Acceptance Criteria

### Primary Scenario

**Given** a ward nurse with a valid care-team relationship opens a patient's encounter in MediCore
**When** the request completes successfully
**Then** exactly one `audit.phi_access.record.read` event is persisted with the actor subject, role, facility, tenant, patient and encounter identifiers, the OpenFGA decision path, the trace ID and both `occurred_at` and `recorded_at`; the event is published to JetStream; and the clinical response latency increases by no more than 3 ms at p95.

### Failure or Validation Scenario

**Given** a clinician activates break-glass access to a patient outside their care team and the business write commits, but NATS JetStream is unavailable
**When** the transactional outbox relay attempts to publish
**Then** the audit record is already durably committed in PostgreSQL alongside the clinical change (so no audit is lost), the outbox row remains undispatched and is retried with backoff, an `audit_outbox_backlog` metric alerts after five minutes, and the break-glass grant itself is not silently extended by the failure.

### Edge Cases

* A CareConnect nurse records a home visit offline and syncs six hours later — the event stores the true `occurred_at` from the device alongside the server `recorded_at`, and clock skew beyond a configured tolerance is flagged rather than corrected.
* A bulk export of 5,000 records produces one `audit.export.completed` event describing the query, count and destination, not 5,000 individual read events.
* A denied access attempt (OpenFGA returns false) is audited with `outcome = deny` — denials are more security-relevant than allows and must never be dropped.
* A developer adds a new entity classified `phi` without implementing the audit interface — the CI coverage gate fails with the entity name.
* A retention partition reaches its Country Profile expiry while a legal hold from an open incident (#53) references it — the drop is refused and the partition is retained until the hold is released.
* The application role attempts `UPDATE audit_event` — the statement is rejected by PostgreSQL privileges, verified by an integration test, not merely by convention.

---

## Engineering Guardrails

Complete the applicable items before the story is closed.

### Code Quality

* [ ] The change is limited to the agreed scope.
* [ ] Existing behaviour remains backward-compatible unless explicitly approved.
* [ ] Code follows the team’s agreed standards and architecture.
* [ ] No temporary code, debug output or unnecessary complexity remains.
* [ ] Error handling is explicit and does not silently ignore failures.

### Test-Driven Development

* [ ] Acceptance criteria were converted into test scenarios.
* [ ] New or changed business logic was developed using Red–Green–Refactor where practical.
* [ ] Bug fixes include a regression test that fails before the fix and passes afterwards.
* [ ] Tests validate behaviour rather than private implementation details.

### Automated Testing

* [ ] Unit tests cover new and changed logic.
* [ ] Positive, negative and important boundary scenarios are covered.
* [ ] Integration or contract tests are updated where service boundaries change.
* [ ] Critical user journeys are covered by Playwright or an equivalent E2E framework.
* [ ] Existing tests pass.
* [ ] No new flaky or skipped tests are introduced without justification.

### Security and Access

* [ ] Authentication and authorisation are enforced at the appropriate layer.
* [ ] Users and services can access only the data and actions they require.
* [ ] Input is validated and sensitive information is not exposed in logs or errors.
* [ ] Secrets and credentials are not stored in source code.
* [ ] Security and dependency scans pass.
* [ ] Tenant, account or customer isolation is tested where applicable.

### Accessibility and User Journey

* [ ] The primary user journey works from start to completion.
* [ ] Loading, empty, success and error states are handled.
* [ ] Keyboard navigation and focus behaviour work correctly.
* [ ] Controls have clear labels and accessible names.
* [ ] The change meets the team’s agreed WCAG accessibility level.
* [ ] The experience works across supported devices and browsers.

### Performance and Reliability

* [ ] The change does not introduce unnecessary API calls, database queries or processing.
* [ ] Timeouts, retries and failure behaviour are defined where applicable.
* [ ] Duplicate requests do not create inconsistent data.
* [ ] Performance-sensitive changes are tested against an agreed threshold.
* [ ] Partial failures do not leave the system in an invalid state.

### Observability

* [ ] Important failures are logged with useful diagnostic context.
* [ ] Logs do not contain sensitive information.
* [ ] Metrics or traces are added where the change affects a critical workflow.
* [ ] The team can determine whether the feature is working correctly after deployment.

### Documentation

* [ ] Relevant README, API or technical documentation is updated.
* [ ] Configuration or environment changes are documented.
* [ ] Deployment, migration or rollback steps are documented where required.
* [ ] Known limitations are recorded.

---

## Result

* **Expected user or system outcome:** every classified read and write across all products produces a canonical, attributable, append-only audit record, with zero unaudited PHI access paths detectable by the coverage gate.
* **Expected business or operational outcome:** hospitals can answer accreditation assessors and data-principal requests about who accessed a record; break-glass becomes a reviewable control rather than an unmonitored bypass; #52, #55, #436 and #437 are unblocked.
* **Success metric or validation method:** 100% of entities classified PHI or PII covered by the emission gate in CI; zero audit events lost across a forced JetStream outage drill (verified by reconciling outbox rows against stored events); p95 added request latency ≤ 3 ms and p99 ≤ 8 ms under a 2,000 rps read benchmark; zero raw PHI values present in `changes` payloads across a sampled 100,000-event scan.
* **Monitoring period:** 60 days post-deployment, with the outbox backlog and audit-emission-rate metrics reviewed weekly.

---

## Pull Request Evidence

The pull request should include:

* [ ] Link to this story.
* [ ] Summary of the change.
* [ ] Test evidence.
* [ ] Screenshots or recordings for UI changes.
* [ ] Security, accessibility or performance evidence where relevant.
* [ ] Deployment and rollback notes for higher-risk changes.
* [ ] Known risks or follow-up work.

---

## Definition of Done

The story is complete when:

* [ ] All acceptance criteria pass.
* [ ] Required tests pass locally and in CI.
* [ ] No critical or high-severity security or quality issues remain.
* [ ] The critical user or system journey has been validated.
* [ ] Documentation is updated.
* [ ] Code review is complete.
* [ ] The change has been deployed or is ready for deployment through the standard pipeline.
* [ ] Post-deployment validation is defined or completed.
* [ ] Any exception is documented with an owner and reason.

---

## Exceptions

**Guardrail:** Accessibility and User Journey — the entire section.
**Reason:** this story delivers a backend emission library, a transactional outbox relay and a storage schema. It ships no user interface; the surfaces that render audit data to humans are #55 and #437, where the accessibility guardrails apply in full.
**Alternative validation:** the developer-facing journey is validated instead — a Go integration test that adds a new classified entity and asserts the CI coverage gate produces an actionable failure message naming the entity and the missing interface.
**Residual risk:** none material for this story; the risk transfers to #55 and #437, which carry the guardrail unexempted.
**Approved by:** Security Lead and Platform Architect.

items.title: ASSPS master coordination: four workstreams, chat consolidation and release ownership
items.body:
# Central agent handoff — 8 October 2026

**Read first:** [ASSPS consolidated governance report](https://github.com/HassiMian/app-assps-edu-pk/blob/coord/assps-four-stream-consolidation-20261008/docs/coordination/CHAT_CONSOLIDATION_AND_AGENT_GOVERNANCE_20261008.md) and the four `*_MASTER_HANDOFF.md` documents on the same documentation-only branch.

Only four active development chat/workstreams: (1) Paper Studio, including Paper Workspace, printing, Early Years, Lesson Planning, Diary and approved bank **consumption**; (2) Grade IX–X Academic Question Bank, independently verified provenance and **approval**; (3) SaaS Core & Production, sole release/DB/RLS owner; (4) APEX Connect, role-aware SaaS client/projection, **not** separate source-of-truth.

**Observed, not permanent:** live frontend `9fe7b560`, backend `16ab8f34` on 2026-10-08 13:08Z; release anchor `68a158e`. Grade 9/10 research `1b29218` not academically approved. Lesson/Diary candidate `2b10eab` not deployed. This handoff only documents ownership; production untouched.

**Every agent must preflight:** verify live component metadata, source ancestry and clean worktrees; claim feature paths/owner; preserve other agents' work; record exact test/role/RLS/print and rollback evidence. Core alone promotes to production after gates. The Academic stream sends only independently approved revision-bound snapshots to Paper Studio. Never use old chat instructions as deployment authority.

Related unfinished issues: [#1](https://github.com/HassiMian/app-assps-edu-pk/issues/1) Curriculum-Paper contract, [#2](https://github.com/HassiMian/app-assps-edu-pk/issues/2) Phase3AE, [#3](https://github.com/HassiMian/app-assps-edu-pk/issues/3) serial+statement selection. Do not close them merely because this coordination issue exists.

**Chat history:** Group eligible old chats in ChatGPT Projects, keep one MASTER per stream, archive rather than delete after unique-history verification. These docs are NOT a physical ChatGPT chat merge; no automatic confirmation of other independent agents receiving or acknowledging this notice.

items.body:
# Full-stack Engineering Roadmap

A knowledge map for practical senior engineering and technical interviews. Topics range from everyday working knowledge to concepts worth recognizing for future use. Inclusion does not imply equal priority or a requirement to master everything.

Tools are examples of broader concepts. Resources are selected references to consult by topic.

## 1. Fundamentals & Development

### 1.1 Common

- **Computer and OS fundamentals** — CPU, memory, stack and heap, filesystems, processes and threads, scheduling, virtual memory, environment variables, permissions, file descriptors, signals, exit codes.
- **CLI and shell** — navigation, pipes, redirection, quoting, text processing, searching files, shell scripting, process management, remote access, troubleshooting disk, memory, and network usage.
- **Networking** — IP addresses, ports, sockets, DNS, TCP, UDP, HTTP/HTTPS, TLS, SSH, proxies, connection reuse, HTTP versions, request/response lifecycle, latency and bandwidth.
- **Programming foundations** — values and types, control flow, functions, scope, modules, references and mutation, equality, error handling, iteration, recursion, imperative, object-oriented, and functional programming.
- **Concurrency and execution** — synchronous and asynchronous execution, blocking and nonblocking I/O, concurrency and parallelism, threads, event loops, race conditions, synchronization, cancellation, resource cleanup.
- **Everyday correctness** — Unicode and encodings, dates and time zones, floating-point precision, decimal arithmetic for money, serialization, nullability, input validation, numerical limits, deterministic behavior.
- **Git and collaboration workflows** — commits, branches, merges, rebasing, conflict resolution, cherry-picking, revert/reset, stash, reflog, bisect, tags, pull requests, code review, branching strategies.
- **Dependencies and environments** — package managers, dependency resolution, lockfiles, semantic versioning, runtime versions, environment configuration, reproducible builds, dependency updates, supply-chain risks.
- **Debugging** — reproducing failures, minimal reproductions, hypotheses, stack traces, breakpoints, inspecting state, logs, source maps, regression isolation, memory leaks, race conditions, debugging across boundaries.
- **Testing** — unit, integration, component, contract, E2E, smoke, regression, and accessibility testing; test doubles, fixtures, test data, deterministic tests, flaky tests, coverage limitations.
- **Further testing depth** — property-based testing, fuzzing, mutation testing, snapshot tradeoffs, test isolation, compatibility testing, testing concurrent and time-dependent behavior.
- **Performance investigation** — profiling before optimization, CPU versus I/O bottlenecks, memory usage, realistic benchmarks, load/stress/soak tests, percentiles, performance budgets, production versus local behavior.
- **Build and delivery** — linting, formatting, static analysis, CI pipelines, build artifacts, dependency caching, release versioning, environment promotion, deployment checks, feature flags, rollbacks.
- **Containers and infrastructure** — images, containers, Dockerfiles, volumes, container networking, Compose, registries; virtual machines, cloud compute, storage, networking, IAM, infrastructure as code.
- **Orchestration awareness** — Kubernetes workloads, services, configuration, secrets, probes, resource limits, autoscaling; managed platforms and the operational cost of running infrastructure.
- **Documentation and communication** — usable READMEs, setup instructions, API documentation, diagrams, change logs, issue reports, review feedback, onboarding, explaining technical decisions.
- **Engineering ownership** — clarifying requirements, acceptance criteria, estimating uncertainty, splitting work, communicating risk, managing dependencies, reviewing others’ work, mentoring, following changes through production.

**Resources**

- [roadmap.sh — Backend](https://roadmap.sh/backend) and [Frontend](https://roadmap.sh/frontend) — broad coverage references.
- [Pro Git](https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2) — Git concepts, internals, and workflows.
- [OWASP Cheat Sheet Series](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/) — practical security guidance across application development.

### 1.2 Frontend

- **Browser internals** — navigation, resource loading, HTML parsing, DOM, CSSOM, critical rendering path, layout, paint, compositing, browser processes, network waterfalls.
- **HTML and native behavior** — semantic elements, document structure, forms, validation, buttons and links, tables, media, dialogs, native interactions, progressive enhancement.
- **CSS foundations** — cascade, specificity, inheritance, box model, positioning, stacking contexts, units, sizing, overflow, selectors, custom properties, cascade layers.
- **Layout and responsive interfaces** — Flexbox, Grid, responsive design, media and container queries, typography, logical properties, responsive images, animation, reduced motion.
- **CSS organization** — naming conventions, scoped styles, CSS Modules, utility classes, preprocessors, CSS-in-JS, design tokens, theming, maintainability and runtime tradeoffs.
- **JavaScript fundamentals** — primitive and reference values, coercion, scope, closures, prototypes, `this`, classes, modules, destructuring, iterables, generators, errors.
- **JavaScript execution** — call stack, tasks and microtasks, promises, async/await, event loop, concurrency limits, cancellation, garbage collection, memory retention.
- **TypeScript** — inference, narrowing, unions and intersections, generics, discriminated unions, utility types, mapped and conditional types, declaration files, module resolution, compiler configuration.
- **Type boundaries** — `unknown` versus `any`, type assertions, structural typing, runtime validation, schema-derived types, checking external data; compile-time types do not validate runtime inputs.
- **DOM and browser APIs** — DOM updates, event propagation and delegation, Fetch, AbortController, URL and History APIs, observers, file APIs, clipboard, permissions.
- **Browser storage and offline behavior** — cookies, localStorage/sessionStorage, IndexedDB, storage quotas, service workers, cache storage, offline fallbacks, update behavior, cross-tab communication.
- **React fundamentals** — components, props, state, state snapshots, batching, keys and identity, render/commit phases, hooks, effects and cleanup, refs, context, controlled and uncontrolled inputs.
- **React behavior and performance** — stale closures, effect dependencies, derived state, error boundaries, Suspense, transitions, memoization tradeoffs, profiling, reconciliation; Fiber as deeper implementation knowledge.
- **Application state and data flow** — local, shared, URL, and server state; routing, forms, validation, fetching, caching, invalidation, optimistic updates, pagination, infinite scrolling, request races.
- **User-facing states** — loading, empty, partial, error, retry, offline, and permission-denied states; preserving user input, preventing duplicate actions, cancellation, recovery.
- **Rendering strategies** — CSR, SSR, SSG, incremental regeneration, streaming, hydration, server/client component boundaries, routing and data loading, caching and revalidation.
- **Accessibility** — keyboard navigation, focus management, accessible names, semantic controls, screen readers, ARIA, contrast, zoom, reduced motion, accessible forms and dynamic feedback.
- **Frontend tooling** — bundlers, transpilers, ESM/CommonJS interoperability, source maps, tree shaking, code splitting, asset pipelines, development servers, build caching, browser compatibility.
- **Frontend performance** — Core Web Vitals, real-user and lab measurements, bundle analysis, lazy loading, image/font optimization, long tasks, rendering bottlenecks, list virtualization, memory leaks.
- **Frontend testing** — behavior-focused component tests, user interactions, network mocking, visual regression, accessibility checks, cross-browser testing, hydration and routing failures.
- **Internationalization and SEO** — translations, pluralization, locale-aware formatting, right-to-left layouts, metadata, canonical URLs, structured data, sitemaps, crawlability, indexing.
- **Browser security boundaries** — same-origin policy, CORS behavior, CSP, safe DOM insertion, cookie attributes, iframe isolation, cross-window messaging, handling untrusted content.
- **Further depth** — Web Components, Shadow DOM, Web Workers, WebAssembly, Canvas/WebGL/WebGPU, WebRTC, progressive web apps; applicability and compatibility constraints.

**Resources**

- [MDN Learn Web Development](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn_web_development) — primary foundation for HTML, CSS, JavaScript, accessibility, and browser behavior.
- [TypeScript Handbook](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/intro.html) — language and type-system reference.
- [React documentation](https://react.dev/learn) — component, state, rendering, and effect mental models.
- [web.dev Learn](https://web.dev/learn) — focused material on performance, accessibility, forms, and modern web capabilities.

### 1.3 Backend

- **Runtime behavior** — request lifecycle, process lifecycle, configuration, connection reuse, resource limits, graceful shutdown, background workers, long-running versus request-scoped execution.
- **Node.js** — event loop, filesystem, streams and backpressure, buffers, events, modules, worker threads, child processes, asynchronous error handling, avoiding CPU-heavy blocking.
- **PHP** — language types, arrays, functions, namespaces, classes, interfaces, traits, enums, exceptions, attributes, Composer, autoloading, common PSRs, PHP-FPM, OPcache, CLI and worker processes.
- **Backend frameworks** — routing, middleware, controllers, validation, dependency containers, ORM integration, serialization, exception handling, queues, scheduling, framework lifecycle and conventions.
- **Relational databases** — modeling, keys, constraints, normalization, joins, aggregations, subqueries, CTEs, window functions, indexes, transactions, isolation levels, locks, deadlocks, query plans.
- **Database access** — connection pools, prepared statements, parameterized queries, ORM/query-builder tradeoffs, N+1 queries, batching, pagination, transaction boundaries, query cancellation.
- **Other storage models** — document, key-value, wide-column, graph, time-series, and search stores; access patterns, query capabilities, operational tradeoffs; Redis data structures and persistence.
- **Data lifecycle** — migrations, backfills, schema compatibility, validation, auditing, retention, deletion, backups, restore testing, data imports/exports, reconciliation.
- **HTTP APIs** — resource modeling, methods, status codes, headers, validation, error formats, pagination, filtering, sorting, versioning, idempotency keys, OpenAPI documentation.
- **Other API styles** — GraphQL schemas and resolvers, query complexity, N+1 prevention; RPC/gRPC and serialization; WebSockets, SSE, polling, connection lifecycle and reconnection.
- **Authentication** — password hashing, sessions, secure cookies, token lifetimes, JWT validation, refresh-token handling, OAuth, OpenID Connect, MFA, passkeys, account recovery.
- **Authorization** — role-based and attribute-based access, resource ownership, tenant scoping, permission checks, least privilege, auditing privileged operations.
- **Application security** — injection, XSS, CSRF, SSRF, path traversal, insecure deserialization, request smuggling awareness, insecure object access, secure headers, secrets and dependency management.
- **Caching implementation** — HTTP cache headers, conditional requests, application caches, Redis, cache keys, TTLs, eviction, invalidation, preventing sensitive-data leakage between users.
- **Web servers and proxies** — nginx/Apache, reverse proxying, TLS termination, compression, buffering, request limits, connection limits, timeouts, health checks, graceful shutdown.
- **Background processing** — job queues, scheduling, worker concurrency, retries, exponential backoff and jitter, dead-letter handling, deduplication, job progress, cancellation.
- **Messaging and streaming** — producers, consumers, acknowledgments, consumer groups, offsets, ordering, redelivery, schema evolution; distinctions between job queues, pub/sub, and retained event logs.
- **Third-party integrations** — timeouts, quotas, webhook signatures, replay protection, duplicate/out-of-order events, reconciliation, sandbox environments, dependency outages.
- **Files and object storage** — uploads/downloads, multipart and resumable uploads, presigned URLs, access control, file validation, malware scanning, metadata, lifecycle rules, CDN delivery.
- **Search and analytics** — inverted indexes, analyzers, relevance, filters, aggregations, reindexing, keeping indexes synchronized, operational versus analytical queries.
- **Observability implementation** — structured logs, metrics, traces, correlation IDs, context propagation, sampling, cardinality, dashboards, alerts, sensitive-data redaction.
- **Operational tooling** — OpenTelemetry for instrumentation; representative monitoring and diagnostic tools such as Prometheus, Grafana, Sentry, and Elasticsearch/Kibana.
- **Further depth** — database storage engines, write-ahead logs, MVCC internals, B-tree/LSM storage tradeoffs, connection protocols, runtime profiling, high-throughput stream processing.

**Resources**

- [roadmap.sh — Backend](https://roadmap.sh/backend) — coverage and related topics.
- [Node.js Learn](https://nodejs.org/en/learn/getting-started/introduction-to-nodejs) and [PHP Manual](https://www.php.net/manual/en/) — runtime and language references.
- [PostgreSQL documentation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/tutorial.html) — SQL foundations, followed by the documentation’s deeper database chapters.
- [OWASP Cheat Sheet Series](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/) — authentication, authorization, validation, and secure implementation guidance.

## 2. Software Design, System Design & Architecture

### 2.1 Software Design / LLD

- **Requirements into design** — use cases, business rules, constraints, invariants, edge cases, state transitions, acceptance criteria, separating essential behavior from implementation choices.
- **Responsibilities and boundaries** — cohesion, coupling, information hiding, encapsulation, separation of concerns, stable interfaces, dependency direction, change isolation.
- **Object-oriented design** — objects, interfaces, polymorphism, composition, inheritance tradeoffs, substitutability, object lifetimes, avoiding excessive hierarchies.
- **Functional design** — pure functions, immutability, higher-order functions, explicit effects, functional core/imperative shell, transformations and pipelines.
- **Design principles** — SOLID, DRY, KISS, YAGNI, least knowledge, command-query separation; conflicting principles, premature abstraction, deliberate duplication.
- **Dependency management** — dependency injection, inversion of control, explicit construction, dependency inversion, service-locator tradeoffs, avoiding hidden global state.
- **Domain modeling** — entities, value objects, aggregates, domain services, domain events, invariants, rich versus anemic models, transaction scripts where appropriate.
- **Interfaces and contracts** — preconditions, postconditions, validation boundaries, error contracts, DTOs, serialization boundaries, version compatibility, making invalid states harder to represent.
- **Creational patterns** — factory, abstract factory, builder, prototype; singleton tradeoffs and alternatives to global mutable state.
- **Structural patterns** — adapter, facade, decorator, proxy, composite, bridge; integration boundaries and wrapping unstable dependencies.
- **Behavioral patterns** — strategy, observer, command, state, template method, chain of responsibility, iterator, mediator, visitor; choosing patterns from actual variation.
- **Persistence patterns** — repository, data mapper, active record, unit of work, identity map; separating domain behavior from persistence without unnecessary layers.
- **Error and resource design** — exceptions versus result types, recoverable versus unrecoverable errors, cleanup, cancellation propagation, ownership of resources, consistent failure behavior.
- **State and concurrency design** — explicit state machines, atomic operations, optimistic/pessimistic concurrency, shared mutable state, lock scope, thread safety.
- **Testability and refactoring** — seams, dependency boundaries, characterization tests, behavior-preserving changes, code smells, simplifying conditional logic, reducing accidental complexity.
- **LLD communication** — class/module relationships, sequence and state diagrams, representative interfaces, tracing a use case through the design, explaining extension points and tradeoffs.

### 2.2 System Design / HLD

- **Problem framing** — users, primary workflows, functional requirements, quality attributes, scope, constraints, assumptions, success criteria.
- **Estimation and capacity** — request rates, peak versus average load, concurrent users, storage growth, bandwidth, cache size, queue depth, headroom, rough cost.
- **Performance models** — latency versus throughput, average versus tail latency, saturation, utilization, bottlenecks, fan-out latency, queueing behavior, Little’s Law.
- **System decomposition** — components, services, responsibilities, data ownership, control flow, data flow, synchronous/asynchronous boundaries, failure boundaries.
- **API and communication choices** — REST, RPC, GraphQL, events, streaming, polling; coupling, compatibility, payload size, serialization, request deadlines.
- **Traffic management** — DNS routing, reverse proxies, L4/L7 load balancing, balancing algorithms, health checks, connection affinity, service discovery, gateways, backends for frontends.
- **Scaling** — vertical and horizontal scaling, stateless services, shared state, partitioning work, autoscaling signals, startup delays, limits imposed by dependencies.
- **Storage selection** — access patterns, relational versus nonrelational models, read/write mix, transactional requirements, durability, indexing, denormalization, materialized views.
- **Replication and partitioning** — leader/follower and multi-leader replication, replica lag, read routing, shard keys, hotspots, rebalancing, consistent hashing, cross-shard queries.
- **Consistency models** — linearizability, eventual and causal consistency, read-your-writes, monotonic reads; transaction isolation versus distributed consistency.
- **Distributed-system limits** — partial failures, network partitions, clock skew, uncertain timeouts, CAP tradeoffs during partitions, coordination costs.
- **Coordination** — leader election, quorum reads/writes and their assumptions, consensus concepts, distributed locks, leases, fencing tokens, unique identifiers.
- **Caching strategy** — cache-aside, read-through, write-through, write-behind, refresh-ahead, invalidation, cache stampedes, hot keys, stale data, multi-layer caches and CDNs.
- **Messaging strategy** — queues versus logs, delivery guarantees, ordering scope, consumer groups, retries, replay, backpressure, poison messages, schema evolution.
- **Distributed workflows** — idempotent operations, transactional outbox/inbox, sagas, orchestration versus choreography, compensating actions; limits and scope of “exactly once” guarantees.
- **Resilience** — timeout budgets, retries with backoff/jitter, circuit breakers, bulkheads, load shedding, graceful degradation, fallbacks, avoiding retry storms.
- **Rate limiting and fairness** — token/leaky buckets, fixed/sliding windows, distributed counters, quotas, admission control, tenant fairness, abuse prevention.
- **Availability and recovery** — redundancy, failover, availability zones and regions, active/passive and active/active designs, disaster recovery, recovery time and recovery point objectives.
- **Security architecture** — trust boundaries, threat modeling, identity propagation, service authentication, tenant isolation, encryption, key management, audit trails, data minimization.
- **Observability and reliability goals** — SLIs, SLOs, error budgets, actionable alerts, distributed tracing, business-level signals, monitoring failure paths.
- **Common design domains** — feeds, chat, notifications, search, file sharing, scheduling, inventory, payments, analytics; recognizing recurring requirements and tradeoffs across domains.
- **HLD interview reasoning** — clarify requirements, estimate only useful quantities, outline the architecture, trace critical flows, identify bottlenecks, examine failure cases, justify choices, adapt to changed constraints.

### 2.3 Architecture in Practice

- **Architectural styles** — layered, modular monolith, hexagonal/ports-and-adapters, clean/onion architecture, service-oriented architecture, microservices, event-driven systems, serverless, pipes and filters.
- **Choosing boundaries** — business capabilities, bounded contexts, ownership, change frequency, deployment independence, data consistency, team structure, avoiding a distributed monolith.
- **Domain-driven design** — ubiquitous language, bounded contexts, context maps, domain versus application services, anti-corruption layers, strategic versus tactical DDD.
- **CQRS and event sourcing** — separating read/write models, projections, event history, replay, event versioning, snapshots, consistency and operational costs; either pattern can exist independently.
- **Frontend architecture** — feature/domain modules, component boundaries, shared UI, design systems, state ownership, routing, data access layers, dependency rules.
- **Frontend delivery architecture** — rendering per route, server/client boundaries, BFFs, edge delivery, microfrontends, monorepos, shared-package versioning, independent deployment tradeoffs.
- **Multi-tenancy** — shared versus isolated infrastructure, tenant-aware data access, schema/database isolation, quotas, customization, noisy neighbors, tenant migrations.
- **Data integration** — change data capture, ETL/ELT, batch and stream processing, schemas, data contracts, lineage, reconciliation, ownership of derived data.
- **Evolving existing systems** — incremental refactoring, strangler migrations, branch by abstraction, parallel runs, compatibility layers, deprecation, avoiding risky rewrites.
- **Safe schema and API changes** — expand/contract migrations, backward/forward compatibility, dual-read/write risks, backfills, contract testing, rollback limitations after data changes.
- **Deployment design** — rolling, blue/green, and canary releases, feature flags, gradual exposure, migration sequencing, rollback versus roll-forward.
- **Operational architecture** — runbooks, incident response, postmortems, failure testing, backup restoration, dependency outage planning, reducing operational toil.
- **Decision-making** — build versus buy, managed versus self-hosted, total ownership cost, vendor lock-in, reversibility, security, maintainability, team capability.
- **Architecture communication** — design proposals, architecture decision records, C4 diagrams, sequence diagrams, alternatives, constraints, risks, review feedback.
- **Technical leadership** — setting standards, facilitating design reviews, prioritizing technical debt, negotiating scope, coordinating changes across teams, mentoring through decisions.
- **Further depth** — service meshes, sidecars, cell-based isolation, multi-region conflict resolution, CRDTs for convergent replicated state, stream-processing time semantics, formal specifications and model checking.

**Resources**

- [roadmap.sh — Software Design & Architecture](https://roadmap.sh/software-design-architecture) and [System Design](https://roadmap.sh/system-design) — main coverage references.
- [Martin Fowler’s Software Architecture Guide](https://martinfowler.com/architecture/) — design boundaries, architectural decisions, and system evolution.
- [Designing Data-Intensive Applications](https://dataintensive.net/) — deeper storage and distributed-systems tradeoffs; paid book.
- [Google SRE books](https://sre.google/books/) — reliability and production operations; free online editions are linked there.
- [C4 model](https://c4model.com/) — communicating architecture at different levels of detail.

## 3. DSA & Problem Solving

### 3.1 Foundations and Complexity

- **Mathematical foundations** — logarithms, powers, sets, basic combinatorics, probability, sequences, summations, modular arithmetic.
- **Complexity notation** — Big O, Θ, and Ω; best, average, and worst cases; amortized analysis; time versus auxiliary space.
- **Analyzing code** — loops, nested loops, recursive calls, call-stack space, recurrence relations, divide-and-conquer complexity, costs hidden in library operations.
- **Correctness reasoning** — invariants, preconditions/postconditions, induction, termination, counterexamples, reasoning about boundaries and state changes.
- **Representation choices** — contiguous versus linked storage, locality, allocation overhead, mutability, ordering, sparse versus dense data, preprocessing versus query cost.
- **Language-specific costs** — strings and slicing, copying, maps and sets, sorting comparators, recursion limits, integer precision/overflow, available priority queues; JS number and bitwise-operation behavior.

### 3.2 Data Structures

- **Arrays and strings** — indexing, resizing, insertion/deletion costs, multidimensional arrays, substring/subsequence distinctions, character encoding.
- **Linked lists** — singly/doubly linked lists, sentinel nodes, reversal, cycle detection, pointer manipulation.
- **Stacks, queues, and deques** — LIFO/FIFO behavior, circular buffers, expression processing, traversal, monotonic structures.
- **Hash maps and sets** — hash functions, collisions, chaining/open addressing, load factor, resizing, expected versus worst-case costs.
- **Trees** — binary trees, binary search trees, traversals, height/depth, balanced trees, ordered operations, lowest common ancestor.
- **Heaps and priority queues** — min/max heaps, heap construction, insertion/removal, top-k problems, merging ordered streams, scheduling.
- **Tries** — prefix lookup, autocomplete, dictionary matching, compressed tries, memory tradeoffs.
- **Graphs** — directed/undirected, weighted/unweighted, adjacency lists/matrices, degrees, paths, cycles, connectivity, DAGs.
- **Disjoint-set union** — union/find, path compression, union by rank/size, connectivity and component tracking.
- **Range-query structures** — prefix sums, difference arrays, Fenwick trees, segment trees, sparse tables; static versus dynamic queries.

### 3.3 Algorithms and Patterns

- **Searching** — linear and binary search, lower/upper bounds, binary search on an answer, monotonic predicates, rotated or partially ordered inputs.
- **Sorting and selection** — insertion, selection, bubble, merge, quick, and heap sort; stability, in-place behavior, counting/radix sort, quickselect, comparison-sort limits.
- **Two pointers** — converging pointers, same-direction pointers, partitioning, merging, sorted-input reasoning.
- **Sliding windows** — fixed/variable windows, frequency tracking, maintaining validity, conditions under which the pattern applies.
- **Prefix techniques** — prefix/suffix aggregates, range queries, prefix sums with hash maps, difference arrays.
- **Intervals and sweeps** — merging, overlap detection, scheduling, event ordering, sweep-line reasoning.
- **Recursion and backtracking** — base cases, decision trees, choose/explore/undo, pruning, combinations, permutations, subsets.
- **Divide and conquer** — splitting problems, combining solutions, recursive decomposition, recurrence analysis.
- **Greedy methods** — local choices, exchange arguments, ordering strategies, recognizing when greediness fails.
- **Dynamic programming** — states, transitions, base cases, memoization, tabulation, reconstruction, space optimization; sequence, grid, knapsack, interval, tree, and bitmask DP.
- **Tree algorithms** — recursive/iterative traversals, subtree information, path problems, tree diameter, BST properties, serialization/deserialization.
- **Graph traversal** — BFS, DFS, connected components, cycle detection, bipartite checking, topological sorting, grid traversal.
- **Shortest paths and spanning trees** — BFS for unweighted paths, Dijkstra for nonnegative weights, Bellman–Ford, Floyd–Warshall, A*, Kruskal, Prim; assumptions and applicability.
- **Heap and monotonic patterns** — top-k, two heaps, k-way merge, monotonic stacks/queues, next-greater elements.
- **String algorithms** — prefix matching, KMP, Z algorithm, rolling hashes, collision awareness, palindrome techniques.
- **Bit manipulation** — bit masks, shifts, XOR, set/clear/test operations, subset representation, signedness and integer-width limits.
- **Number-theoretic algorithms** — GCD/Euclid, prime testing, sieves, fast exponentiation, modular arithmetic.
- **Further depth** — strongly connected components, bridges/articulation points, maximum flow, matching, suffix arrays/trees, balanced-tree internals, randomized algorithms, computational geometry.
- **Practical specialized structures** — Bloom filters for approximate membership, LRU/LFU caches, skip lists, B/B+ trees for storage indexes; false positives, eviction behavior, and workload tradeoffs.
- **Computational limits** — tractable versus intractable problems, P/NP awareness, reductions, exponential search, approximation and heuristics.

### 3.4 Interview Reasoning and Engineering Use

- **Problem clarification** — input constraints, duplicates, ordering, mutability, output requirements, invalid inputs, memory limits.
- **Solution development** — establish a baseline, identify repeated work, recognize useful structure, compare alternatives, explain the invariant.
- **Implementation discipline** — clear naming, manageable state, boundary handling, consistent indexing, avoiding unnecessary cleverness.
- **Validation** — empty/singleton inputs, duplicates, extremes, disconnected graphs, skewed trees, cycles, adversarial ordering, overflow, recursion depth.
- **Communication** — explain assumptions, justify correctness, analyze time/space, discuss alternatives, respond to hints, adapt when constraints change.
- **Engineering judgment** — select structures from actual access patterns, account for constants and locality, prefer maintained libraries when appropriate, profile real bottlenecks.

**Resources**

- [roadmap.sh — Data Structures & Algorithms](https://roadmap.sh/datastructures-and-algorithms) — coverage reference.
- [MIT 6.006: Introduction to Algorithms](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-006-introduction-to-algorithms-spring-2020/) — structured foundations and algorithmic reasoning; examples use Python.
- [CP-Algorithms](https://cp-algorithms.com/) — deeper algorithm reference; many implementations use C++.
- [LeetCode Top Interview 150](https://leetcode.com/studyplan/top-interview-150/) — an optional interview-pattern reference, without treating the problem count as a completion requirement.

## 4. AI-Assisted Development & AI Products

### 4.1 Shared AI Foundations

- **AI landscape** — machine learning, deep learning, generative AI, language models, embedding models, multimodal models; training, adaptation, and inference.
- **How language models work** — tokenization, next-token prediction, embeddings, attention/transformers at a conceptual level, context windows, training knowledge versus supplied information.
- **Capabilities and limitations** — probabilistic outputs, hallucinations, outdated knowledge, instruction sensitivity, unreliable self-assessment, reasoning limitations, task-specific strengths.
- **Model selection** — quality on representative tasks, latency, cost, context capacity, supported modalities, tool use, structured output, privacy, hosted versus local deployment.
- **Generation controls** — output limits, sampling parameters where supported, stop conditions, streaming, reasoning budgets where available; behavior varies by model.
- **Prompting foundations** — clear goals, constraints, examples, relevant context, output requirements, task decomposition, iterative improvement.
- **Context engineering** — selecting useful information, source quality, ordering, freshness, retrieval, summarization, compaction, context isolation, avoiding irrelevant or conflicting material.

### 4.2 Engineering Software with AI

- **Working modes** — autocomplete, conversational assistance, repository-aware agents, terminal/IDE workflows, background tasks; choosing a mode appropriate to task size and risk.
- **Task specification** — desired behavior, scope, constraints, acceptance criteria, relevant files, reproduction steps, examples, definition of completion.
- **Repository understanding** — architecture, entry points, dependencies, conventions, existing implementations, build commands, tests, ownership boundaries.
- **Persistent project guidance** — repository instructions, coding conventions, architectural constraints, test commands, scoped rules, reusable skills and task templates.
- **Planning changes** — exploration before editing, surfacing assumptions, splitting work, identifying dependencies, recording decisions, revisiting plans after new evidence.
- **Context management during work** — relevant file selection, targeted search, documentation retrieval, concise handoffs, checkpoint summaries, avoiding stale assumptions.
- **Implementation workflow** — small coherent changes, inspecting diffs, preserving existing behavior, limiting unrelated edits, integrating with established patterns.
- **AI-assisted debugging** — reproducing the failure, collecting evidence, evaluating hypotheses, tracing execution, separating causes from symptoms, verifying the actual fix.
- **AI-assisted testing** — tests derived from requirements, boundary and failure cases, regression protection, checking that tests can fail for the right reasons.
- **Review and verification** — correctness, security, maintainability, dependency validity, performance implications, type checks, tests, runtime inspection, visual checks where relevant.
- **Tool access and boundaries** — filesystem, terminal, browser, databases, external services, sandboxing, secret handling, network access, approval for consequential actions.
- **Parallel and delegated work** — independent task boundaries, explicit ownership, isolated worktrees, shared contracts, integration review, avoiding concurrent edits to the same code.
- **Long-running work** — checkpoints, resumable progress, task state, budgets, stopping conditions, blocked-state handling, recovery after interruption.
- **Workflow automation** — repeatable reviews, maintenance, documentation updates, issue triage, CI integration, logs, failure reporting, human review points.
- **Failure modes** — invented APIs, unnecessary dependencies, scope drift, plausible but incorrect fixes, over-abstraction, weakening tests, ignoring local conventions.
- **Measuring usefulness** — accepted changes, defects, rework, review effort, cycle time, maintainability; distinguishing generated volume from useful outcomes.
- **Knowledge retention** — reading and explaining generated changes, checking sources, preserving architectural understanding, taking ownership of the resulting code.

**Resources**

- [OpenAI coding-agent best practices](https://learn.chatgpt.com/guides/best-practices) — context, instructions, planning, and verification.
- [Claude Code best practices](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices) — practical agent-assisted development habits.
- [Anthropic: Effective Context Engineering](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents) — managing information across agent workflows.

### 4.3 Building AI-Powered Products

- **Product fit** — user need, expected value, acceptable errors, deterministic alternatives, automation boundaries, human review, measurable product outcomes.
- **Common capabilities** — classification, extraction, summarization, rewriting, semantic search, question answering, recommendations, document understanding, workflow assistance.
- **Application integration** — model APIs and SDKs, server-side credentials, request construction, streaming, cancellation, retries, rate limits, timeouts, error handling.
- **Structured outputs** — schemas, constrained generation where available, parsing, validation, repair/fallback paths; valid structure does not establish factual correctness.
- **Tool/function calling** — tool descriptions, input schemas, dispatch, result handling, validation, authorization, side effects, idempotency, tool failures.
- **Prompt and configuration lifecycle** — versioned prompts, reusable templates, configuration separation, experiments, regression checks, controlled rollout.
- **Conversation and memory** — session state, history selection, summaries, persistent memory, user preferences, consent, expiry, correction and deletion, cross-user isolation.
- **Embeddings and similarity** — vector representations, distance metrics, semantic similarity, embedding-model selection, dimensionality, batch processing, model-version compatibility.
- **Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)** — ingestion, parsing, chunking, metadata, embedding, indexing, retrieval, context construction, grounded answers, citations.
- **Retrieval quality** — lexical versus semantic search, hybrid retrieval, reranking, query rewriting, metadata filters, deduplication, relevance thresholds, coverage and freshness.
- **Knowledge lifecycle** — document updates/deletions, permissions at retrieval time, index synchronization, re-embedding, provenance, conflicting sources, inaccessible information.
- **Vector storage** — vector-capable databases versus dedicated stores, approximate nearest-neighbor indexes, filtering, index tuning, operational cost.
- **Workflows and agents** — fixed pipelines, routing, parallel steps, agent loops, planning, tool selection, state machines, human handoffs; selecting the simplest effective orchestration.
- **Agent reliability** — step/time/cost limits, stopping criteria, loop detection, durable state, checkpoints, replay, recovery, side-effect deduplication.
- **Multi-agent systems** — specialization, delegation, shared versus isolated context, coordination, handoff contracts, integration, additional latency and failure modes.
- **MCP and integrations** — Model Context Protocol hosts, clients, servers, tools, resources, prompts, transports, authentication, scoped permissions, trusted-server selection.
- **Evaluation design** — representative datasets, realistic task distributions, expected behavior, measurable success criteria, edge cases, adversarial inputs, held-out cases.
- **Evaluation methods** — deterministic checks, human review, model-based judges, pairwise comparisons, rubric quality, judge bias, calibration against human judgments.
- **RAG and agent evaluation** — retrieval relevance/coverage, answer grounding, citation validity, tool selection, argument correctness, task completion, side-effect correctness.
- **Product evaluation** — user satisfaction, successful outcomes, escalation rate, abandonment, correction effort, online experiments, feedback quality.
- **AI security** — prompt injection, malicious retrieved content, untrusted tool output, data exfiltration, excessive permissions, unsafe code execution, output sanitization.
- **Authorization boundaries** — enforce access in application/tool code, separate instructions from untrusted data, isolate tenants, require appropriate approval for consequential actions.
- **Privacy and data handling** — sensitive-data minimization, redaction, retention, deletion, consent, provider data policies, log access, provenance and usage rights.
- **UX for uncertainty** — editable results, source inspection, abstention, clarifying questions, partial results, progress, cancellation, undo, clear automation boundaries.
- **Latency and cost** — token budgets, context size, prompt caching, batching, model routing, concurrency, streaming, time to first token, cost per successful outcome.
- **Production operations** — traces across model/tool calls, prompt/model versions, quality monitoring, rate-limit handling, fallbacks, feature flags, canaries, rollback, provider changes.
- **Multimodal applications** — image/document understanding, OCR, audio transcription, speech generation, realtime voice, video processing, modality-specific evaluation.
- **Framework choices** — direct SDKs versus orchestration frameworks, transparent state and tool handling, portability, debugging, operational overhead.

### 4.4 Further AI Depth

- **Model adaptation** — prompt improvement versus retrieval versus fine-tuning, supervised fine-tuning, parameter-efficient adaptation such as LoRA, preference optimization, distillation.
- **Training-data quality** — labeling, representative examples, contamination/leakage, train/validation/test splits, privacy, model and dataset documentation.
- **Local and self-hosted inference** — model formats, quantization, GPU memory, batching, KV caches, throughput, deployment, model licenses, operational tradeoffs.
- **Advanced retrieval** — query decomposition, document hierarchies, graph-based retrieval, multimodal retrieval, long-context alternatives, context compression.
- **Advanced agent capabilities** — browser/computer use, sandboxed code execution, durable workflows, inter-agent communication, environment feedback, auditability.
- **Reliability research awareness** — distribution shift, robustness, calibration, adversarial evaluation, interpretability limits, benchmark limitations.
- **ML foundations for deeper specialization** — linear algebra, probability, optimization, supervised/unsupervised learning, overfitting, generalization, neural networks; a separate depth path from integrating existing models.

**Resources**

- [roadmap.sh — AI Engineer](https://roadmap.sh/ai-engineer) and [AI Agents](https://roadmap.sh/ai-agents) — main coverage references.
- [Anthropic: Building Effective Agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents) — workflow and agent design patterns.
- [OpenAI: Evaluation Best Practices](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/evaluation-best-practices) — evaluating behavior and detecting regressions.
- [Model Context Protocol documentation](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/getting-started/intro) — integration concepts and protocol reference.

items.title: [T03] Prepare an existing imported artwork for release
items.body:
## Parent

Pipeline: https://github.com/JTBAZ/relay/issues/6
Program: https://github.com/JTBAZ/relay/issues/5
Approved slice: T03.

## What to build

An artist selects retained Patreon media and enters existing release preparation without downloading, reuploading or publicly publishing it to Relay.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] An owned, retained supported Patreon image can be selected from the library and passed to existing preparation using its stable source/version reference.
- [ ] Available caption, source link and audience classification remain attached to preparation.
- [ ] No download/reupload or public Relay publication is required; unsupported or missing media is visibly blocked.
- [ ] Wrong-creator or stale references cannot enter preparation; existing patron gates remain unchanged.
- [ ] Demonstrate the library-to-preparation journey through authenticated operations and the relevant UI.

## Ownership boundaries

**Accountable role:** P1 intake/library manager. This is a role assignment, not a GitHub user assignment.

**Owns:** Private intake, retained asset identity/readiness, source/version association and export behavior for this slice.

**Excluded:** No publication authority, new scheduler, fan entitlement redesign, cross-tenant reuse, or unrelated Patreon queue work.

**Boundary reviewers:** P2 for asset/context consumers; P4 for media preparation; P5 for provenance semantics.

One accountable manager owns the complete slice, including necessary existing API/UI integration and tests. Before dispatch, reconcile current branch evidence and unrelated working-tree changes. Use an isolated worktree and a bounded change scope. Schema/migrations, shared API clients, server/worker registration, application shell/navigation and extension protocols require an integration-lead-assigned writer; request contract changes from the owning manager instead of independently rewriting shared surfaces. Worktree isolation does not grant authority to change another pipeline's semantics. Do not add unrelated prefactoring.

## Verification and dispatch

Use the highest relevant authenticated application seam and existing test prior art in the pipeline specification; verify observable behavior rather than private implementation calls. Record baseline failures, test environment, rollback and remaining limits. Native UI and MCP must use the same authorization and records. Security/approval invariants remain binding.

Status: ready-for-agent. Publication is planning only. No implementation, paid experiments, external posting or deployment has been dispatched. Native GitHub blocking relationships govern availability after a later implementation assignment; a blocker-free ticket is eligible, not automatically running.

items.title: mergeEntities violates the append-only/immutability contract and has no inverse — make merges reversible
items.body:
## Summary

`mergeEntities` is the only operation in Neotoma that mutates stored truth in place and destroys state without recording an inverse. This breaks three stated commitments in `docs/NEOTOMA_MANIFEST.md`, and it is the structural reason no `unmerge` exists: you cannot write an inverse for an operation that deletes its own inputs.

`src/services/entity_split.ts:232` already points at the missing function:

> `"Source entity is already merged; unmerge or split the merge target instead."`

There is no `unmerge`. Grep for `unmerge|undoMerge|revertMerge` returns only that string.

## Manifest commitments violated

| § | Commitment | How merge breaks it |
|---|---|---|
| 5.4 | "Truth is immutable… **Corrections create new observations with higher priority**" | Merge does `UPDATE observations SET entity_id`, rewriting stored rows rather than appending a correcting observation |
| 5.7 | "Full provenance — every field must trace to a source and rule" | After a merge, nothing records that a field arrived via merge. The audit row stores a *count*, not ids |
| 12.2 | "Additive evolution only" | Steps 4 and 6 are hard `DELETE`s |

§16 ("Events are immutable after creation") is also in tension with step 6, which deletes `relationship_snapshots` outright.

## What the merge actually does

`src/services/entity_merge.ts`, inside one transaction:

1. `UPDATE observations SET entity_id = to WHERE entity_id = from AND user_id = ?` — **in-place rewrite**
2–3. Read relationship_observations for both sides; build a dedup set keyed on `relationship_key` (`type:source:target`)
4. `DELETE FROM relationship_observations` for self-loops and rows duplicating an edge the survivor already has — **destructive, unrecorded**
5. `UPDATE relationship_observations SET source_entity_id/target_entity_id/relationship_key` — repoint
6. `DELETE FROM relationship_snapshots WHERE source_entity_id = from OR target_entity_id = from` — **destructive, unrecorded**
7. `UPDATE entities SET merged_to_entity_id, merged_at` — tombstone (correctly last, so edges are never orphaned on partial failure)
8. `INSERT INTO entity_merges (…, observations_rewritten, …)` — audit

### Why the audit row is insufficient

```sql
CREATE TABLE entity_merges (
  id, user_id, from_entity_id, to_entity_id,
  reason, merged_by, observations_rewritten, created_at
)
```

`observations_rewritten` is an **integer count**. To reverse step 1 you would have to re-derive *which* observations moved by joining on `source_id` and assuming nothing else touched them since. Steps 4 and 6 are simply unrecoverable — nothing anywhere records that the absorbed entity independently asserted a now-deleted edge.

The comment on the sibling `entity_splits` table claims over-merges can "be surgically reversed without any content rewrite on observations." That is true of `split_entity` in isolation, but **a split cannot undo a merge**, because the merge already deleted the edges a split would need to restore.

## Secondary bug: merge is tenant-scoped, tombstone is not

Step 1 is scoped `AND user_id = ?`, so a merge moves only the **acting user's** observations. Another contributor's observations on the absorbed entity are left pointing at an entity that step 7 tombstones for everyone.

On a shared graph this silently strands data. Concretely: a shared leads instance with three contributors writing contacts into one graph. A merge by one of them orphans the others' observations on the absorbed record. Worth confirming whether this should be a separate issue.

## Proposed fix

Two options. They are not alternatives — (A) is a prerequisite for (B).

### A. Reversible merge (recommended now)

Additive, no behavior change, small:

1. **Record the full inverse in `entity_merges`** — the moved observation ids, and the complete deleted relationship rows as JSON.
2. **Soft-delete instead of `DELETE`** in steps 4 and 6 — add `deleted_at` / `superseded_by_merge_id`, consistent with how the rest of the system already handles deletion.
3. **Ship `unmerge_entities`** reading that row: repoint observations back, restore soft-deleted edges, clear the tombstone.

**(1) is the piece that cannot be retrofitted.** Once a merge runs without recording what it deleted, that information is gone permanently. Landing (1) alone makes every future merge reversible-in-principle even if (3) ships much later.

### B. Conformant merge (the architecturally correct end state)

Never rewrite `entity_id`. Represent the merge as an **observation** that two entities are the same identity, and let snapshot computation resolve through it. This is what §5.4 actually prescribes — "corrections create new observations" — and it makes unmerge trivial: retract the observation.

Cost: touches every read path that currently assumes `entity_id` is authoritative. Materially larger than (A), and (A)'s audit record is needed regardless.

## Why this matters now

Any dedupe sweep is currently a one-way door. On a shared leads instance the deployed identifier fix (#1982) has begun surfacing genuine duplicate pairs — e.g. two records for one person sharing an email address, one carrying phone + profile URL and the other carrying lead-scoring fields, with neither a subset of the other. Merging those is the obvious cleanup, and today it is unrecoverable if the resolver is wrong about any pair.

That is the practical cost of the gap: the safest available process is "dry-run and eyeball every pair," which does not scale to thousands of contacts.

### Problem statement
`mergeEntities` is the only Neotoma write path that destroys prior state in place instead of appending a correcting fact. It rewrites `observations.entity_id`, hard-deletes `relationship_observations` and `relationship_snapshots` rows, and records only an integer count (`observations_rewritten`) — not the ids or content needed to reconstruct what was deleted. This violates manifest §5.4 (truth is immutable, corrections are additive), §5.7 (full provenance), and §12.2 (additive evolution only), and it is why no `unmerge` exists: nothing records the inverse. Today's only safe mitigation — "dry-run and eyeball every pair" — does not scale, which blocks any dedupe sweep on shared graphs (concretely blocking cleanup of duplicate pairs surfaced by #1982's identifier fix).

### Design / UX

**User goal:** an agent/developer who ran a merge that turned out wrong needs to undo it — same trust bar as any other reversible action in Neotoma: fast, unambiguous, no silent partial-success.

#### Naming
- Tool/operation: **`unmerge_entities`** (not `undo_merge` or `revert_merge`) — matches the existing verb pair `merge_entities` / `split_entity`, and is the exact term `entity_split.ts:232` already promises ("unmerge or split the merge target instead"). Consistent naming here closes a promise the codebase already made.
- Parameter: **`merge_id`** (the `entity_merges` row id), not `from_entity_id`/`to_entity_id` — the merge may have deduped/repointed edges in ways that can't be reconstructed from the two entity ids alone; the merge id is the only correct handle on the specific inverse payload. Passing entity ids instead should error with a hint (below), not silently guess the latest merge.
- REST route: `POST /entities/unmerge` (mirrors `POST /entities/merge`), body `{ "merge_id": "..." }`. `operationId: unmergeEntities`.
- MCP tool: `unmerge_entities`, registered alongside `merge_entities` in `src/tool_definitions.ts`, same section/category so it's discoverable by proximity, not just by grep.

#### Discoverability
- [ ] `merge_entities`' tool description and the `/entities/merge` OpenAPI description gain a one-line pointer: "Reversible — see `unmerge_entities`." An agent that just merged should learn the undo path exists without a second search.
- [ ] The merge **response payload** itself echoes `merge_id` prominently (e.g. top-level field, not buried in an audit object) — this is the value the agent needs to call `unmerge_entities` later, and it must not require a follow-up `retrieve` to find.
- [ ] `unmerge_entities`'s own description states the round-trip guarantee in plain terms: "Reverses a prior merge_entities call: restores the source entity, repoints its observations, and restores any relationship rows the merge deleted or repointed. Requires the merge_id returned by merge_entities."

#### Interaction / flow
1. Agent calls `merge_entities(from, to)` → gets back `{ merge_id, to_entity_id, ... }`.
2. Agent (or a human reviewing the merge later) decides to reverse it → calls `unmerge_entities(merge_id)`.
3. System validates the merge is unmergeable (see error states) → applies inverse → returns confirmation payload.
4. Confirmation payload should let the caller verify the effect without a separate round-trip: echo `restored_entity_id`, `observations_restored: <n>`, `relationships_restored: <n>` — counts here are fine for a human-readable confirmation (unlike the storage layer, which per the eng/PM section above must persist full ids/content, not just counts).

No interactive/UI surface in v1 (confirmed acceptable per PM's open item) — this is API/tool-only, so every state below must be legible from a JSON error response and a one-line tool-result message, since there is no screen to add context.

#### Error states (each needs a specific code + actionable hint, not a generic 400/500)

| Condition | Error | Message (agent-facing) |
|---|---|---|
| `merge_id` doesn't exist | `MERGE_NOT_FOUND` | "No merge found with id `{merge_id}`. Check the `merge_id` returned by the original `merge_entities` call — this is not an entity id." |
| Merge already unmerged | `MERGE_ALREADY_REVERSED` | "Merge `{merge_id}` was already unmerged at `{unmerged_at}`. Nothing to do." (idempotent no-op read, not an error the caller must handle specially — but still surfaced, not silently 200'd with no explanation) |
| Source entity was merged **again** into a third entity after this merge (chained merge) | `MERGE_SUPERSEDED` | "Entity `{from_entity_id}` was merged again into `{other_entity_id}` after this merge. Unmerge that later merge first, or this would leave data in an inconsistent state." — this is the sharpest edge case: chained merges (A→B, then B→C) make naive unmerge of the first merge unsafe. Flagging for arch/eng: does capture at merge time need to detect and block/relate chained merges, or is this pushed to unmerge-time validation only? Either way the error must name the *specific* blocking merge, not just say "cannot unmerge." |
| Inverse record missing/malformed (legacy pre-fix merge, or corruption) | `MERGE_NOT_REVERSIBLE` | "Merge `{merge_id}` predates reversible-merge support (or its inverse record is corrupt) and cannot be automatically undone. No safe partial action was taken." — must fail closed per the acceptance criteria; this message is the one place an agent will hit the "backfill is out of scope" decision live, so it needs to say *why*, not just fail. |
| Concurrent write to source/target entity between merge and unmerge (another observation landed on either entity since) | `MERGE_STALE` (if detected) or silently layered as a new observation (if not) | Arch question: does unmerge need to detect "new data landed on the target after the merge, which observation does it belong to now?" — flagging as an open question rather than asserting a message, since it depends on the capture design above. |
| Caller passes `from_entity_id`/`to_entity_id` instead of `merge_id` | `INVALID_PARAMETER` | "`unmerge_entities` takes `merge_id`, not entity ids — a source entity may have been merged more than once. Find `merge_id` in the original `merge_entities` response or via `list_recent_changes`." |
